Chapter 2: The Night of the Explosion and the First Response
Picture this. Most people are fast asleep. Some are working late, maybe catching up on a shift, while others are celebrating birthdays or just lounging in front of the TV. Everything feels normal—until it isn’t.
Suddenly, there’s a distant rumble. Maybe a strange, almost otherworldly light flickers in the sky. Or your phone rings in the middle of the night with news you never expected. For the workers at the plant, confusion hits hard and fast. Alarms are screaming, but the instructions? They’re muddled and unclear. No one wants to believe what just happened—because it’s unthinkable.
Now, imagine being one of the first firefighters on the scene. One of them would later remember the chaos—how he and his crew raced toward the burning reactor, not having a clue what they were walking into. All they saw were flames and felt heat pressing in on every side. And, just like always, they did what they were trained to do: they fought the fire. There was no mention of radiation. No warning about the kind of danger they couldn’t see. They worked through the night, their faces and hands burning, their uniforms offering no real protection at all.
Meanwhile, back in the city, people stepped out onto balconies, gazing up at that strange, glowing light. Some even thought it was beautiful, never realizing the deadly particles drifting on the breeze. Parents tried to calm their kids, promising everything would be fine. The authorities, not yet understanding just how serious things were, offered reassurances. So, for a few more hours, life carried on almost like nothing had happened.
In the hospital, doctors and nurses were treating the first victims. But what they saw didn’t make sense—burns with no clear cause, symptoms they’d never seen before. The patients—firefighters, plant workers, people who just happened to be nearby—were getting sicker by the hour. Their skin blistered, their hair began to fall out, and their bodies just couldn’t cope. The staff did their best, improvising treatments and trying to hide their own fear.
For the families of those brave responders, the waiting was almost unbearable. Wives and mothers crowded the hospital corridors, desperate for any scrap of news. Some were allowed quick visits, only to be stunned by the changes in their loved ones. The official explanations? Always vague. No one said the word “radiation.” The truth was hidden behind a thick wall of silence.
As dawn finally broke, it got harder and harder to ignore the scale of the disaster. The plant was still burning. The air was heavy with dust. Soldiers arrived and started sealing off the area. Buses lined up, ready to evacuate people from the city, but many just refused to leave. They didn’t really understand the danger. They couldn’t imagine abandoning their homes.
In those first few hours, something else became clear—the gap between what people saw and what they were told was growing wider and wider. This wasn’t just a disaster you could see or touch. It became a crisis of trust. The authorities’ hesitation to share real information left people vulnerable, forced to make impossible decisions with almost no guidance at all. And the scariest part? The threat was invisible. Radiation was everywhere—and nowhere. You couldn’t see it or smell it, but it was deadly all the same.
